background.definition: Acute bacterial prostatitis is a culture-confirmed bacterial urinary tract infection that causes a painful and tender prostate.

list.listitem: Two million annual visits to primary care clinics (1% of all visits) and urology clinics (8% of all visits) are because of prostatitis. However, less than 5% of these are thought to be caused by acute bacterial prostatitis.
The incidence of acute bacterial prostatitis status post transrectal prostate needle biopsy is approximately 1%.
Although the prevalence of prostatitis has been estimated to be as high as 8%, acute bacterial prostatitis accounts for less than 5% of these cases.
$84 million is spent on prostatitis treatment in the United States per year.
Pathogens usually include gram-negative gastrointestinal flora: Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, and Enterococci.
Other potential bacterial causes: Proteus species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus.

It is a relatively common complication of prostate biopsy. These patients are at greater risk for sepsis, and in one series 90% had E. coli as the causative agent (compared with 67% in patients with spontaneous acute prostatitis).

Pathogenic bacteria are thought to arrive at the prostate via 1 of 2 pathways: Intraductal reflux of infected urine: the bacteria then have retrograde flow in the ejaculatory and prostatic ducts and arrive within the prostate. Ascending urethral infection, often following sexual intercourse.
Once pathogenic bacteria infiltrate the prostate, the host mounts an intense inflammatory response.
Prophylactic antibiotics given prior to biopsy (a single dose of ciprofloxacin 750 mg given 2 hours before the procedure) appears to reduce the risk of infection.B
Obtain a urine culture in all patients with suspected acute prostatitis. C
The clinical diagnosis is made on the basis of a urinary tract infection and a tender prostate with or without fever. C
Consider ultrasound to look for evidence of urinary retention. C

Differential.Differential_Features: High-risk sexual behavior, urethral discharge, skin lesions
May be incidental finding on urine screening
Nontender prostate, pain with bladder filling

list.listitem: Most patients present with a combination of fever, urinary symptoms, and abnormal digital rectal examination. Urinary symptoms include bladder outlet obstruction, dysuria, macroscopic hematuria, and burning with micturition.
Patients with acute bacterial prostatitis following transrectal prostate biopsy are typically older, have a higher peak fever, and are more likely to have signs of sepsis.
The patient may also complain of perineal and pelvic pain, including pain with defecation and ejaculation.

Physical examination is critical to diagnosis; digital rectal examination often shows a tender, warm, swollen, and firm prostate. Palpation should not be vigorous because of the theoretical risk of sepsis, and prostatic massage is contraindicated when acute prostatitis is suspected because of an increased risk of sepsis.
Urinalysis is consistent with a urinary tract infection, including positive leukocyte esterase and bacteriuria.
It has been recommended that residual volume should be assessed with ultrasound in patients with acute bacterial prostatitis.
A failed course of antibiotic treatment or fluctuation noted on prostatic examination should be followed up with transrectal ultrasound to evaluate for a prostatic abscess.

If the abscess has penetrated the confines of the prostate gland, or if you suspect abscess extension beyond the prostate, additional imaging via CT or MRI may be required. CT is helpful to assess tissue and gas surrounding the prostate, but MRI better evaluates infection near the prostate.

Prostate specific antigen (PSA) levels often become elevated with prostatitis and remain elevated for 2 to 3 months. If a screening PSA is elevated during this time, it should be repeated in 2 to 3 months following resolution of prostatitis.
Suspect acute bacterial prostatitis in a male patient with signs and symptoms of urinary tract infection, fever, and a tender prostate on examination.
Consider an ultrasound of the bladder to detect urinary retention; a urine culture should also be obtained (see ).
If the patient has not improved with empiric antibiotic treatment, a transrectal ultrasound should be considered to evaluate for prostatic abscess.

Start empiric antibiotics (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin for 2-4 weeks) immediately when prostatitis is suspected. Public Health England guidelines recommend 28 days for acute prostatitis.C
When residual urine is noted, use an alpha-receptor blocker. C
When urinary retention is present, insert a single-use or indwelling suprapubic catheter for definitive treatment. C

Antibiotic coverage should include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or a fluoroquinolone for 2 to 4 weeks. Guidelines from Public Health England recommend a 28 day course of treatment for acute prostatitis. The optimal duration of treatment has not been well studied; 40% of urologists and 65% of primary care physicians treat patients for only 2 weeks.
A study of English prescriptions for acute prostatitis found that 12.5% were for longer than 28 days, while 52% were for less than 28 days including 26% for less than 14 days.
In 272 men with afebrile UTI (which likely included some men with prostate involvement) 7 days of antibiotics was similarly effective to 14 days.
Of the fluoroquinolones, ciprofloxacin and norfloxacin have the best prostatic penetration.
Fosfomycin is another option although has been less well studied than other antibiotics. In a single study with 18 patients, all had clinical cure and all but one had microbiological cure.
If there is residual urine on imaging or irritative voiding symptoms, there may be a benefit to alpha-blocker therapy.
If urinary retention is present, a single-use or indwelling suprapubic catheter should be used.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or acetaminophen and stool softeners or laxatives may be beneficial in reducing patients' symptoms.

Abscesses smaller than 1 cm should be treated with antibiotic therapy as well as with the placement of a suprapubic catheter and regular ultrasound imaging. If an abscess is identified, antibiotics that cover anaerobes (such as clindamycin) should be considered.
Prostatic abscesses of 1 cm or larger should be drained.

Surgical options for definitive abscess treatment include transurethral incision or resection, suprapubic adenectomy, perineal incision, and transrectal or transperineal prostatic puncture and drainage performed using transrectal ultrasound.
Studies on rats suggest soy may play a protective role.
Patients may need to be hospitalized when serious infections develop, including prostatic abscess (3% of patients with prostatitis) and rarely, urosepsis.
The incidence of abscess increases when prostatitis is presumed to be secondary to prostatic manipulation.
Urinary retention is a potentially serious complication that can be evaluated via bladder scan.
If retention is noted, a single-use or indwelling suprapubic catheter should be placed.
Recurrence develops in approximately 1 in 8 patients. B
Therapy is more likely to fail in individuals with hyperplasia, anatomic abnormalities, history of urinary catheterization, or neurogenic bladder.
Complications include acute urinary retention, epididymitis, prostatic abscess, urosepsis, and chronic bacterial prostatitis.
The relapse rate is approximately 13%.
Therapeutic success is more common in those with hematuria and a tender prostate.
Therapeutic failure is more likely to occur in individuals with hyperplasia, anatomic abnormalities, history of urinary catheterization, or neurogenic bladder.
Epidemiologic studies have found an association between acute bacterial prostatitis and prostate cancer. However, this may be due to ascertainment bias or other confounders.
Patients with biopsy-associated acute prostatitis are at greater risk for sepsis and are more likely to have E. coli as the causative agent.
Sensitivities to empirically prescribed antibiotics should be confirmed via urine culture.
If the bacteria are resistant to the empiric antibiotic, the regimen should be altered and continued for a subsequent 2 to 4 weeks.
